Why we started NEUVELIF
After every skin procedure, I was left with the same question.

The procedure went well,
but now what should I use, and how?
A note from our CEO
I looked for answers, and every source said something different
A skin procedure ends at the clinic, but skincare starts at home that same day. Yet it was hard to know when to start after a procedure, what to use, and how.

When I looked for answers, the information was all over the place. Some said you could apply products the same day; others said to put nothing on your skin for several days. Not knowing what to trust, I usually ended up just using whatever I normally used.
Products made for everyday skin
But most skincare products are made with everyday skin in mind. So after a procedure, even the products you always use become hard to use.
Why skincare is hard after a skin procedure
Products that sting or burn
Many products sting or burn when applied to sensitized skin.
Rubbing and foaming
Rubbing, foaming, and massaging motions are often things to avoid after a skin procedure.
Ingredients you need to pause
Some products contain ingredients you need to pause for a while after a procedure, such as exfoliants or retinol.
No guidance on timing
It's hard to find products that tell you when and how you can use them after a procedure.
So I decided to make them myself
I couldn't find the answer, so I decided to make it myself.
NEUVELIF was created to solve this problem. We make skincare designed around skin that has become sensitive before and after procedures, and we tell you when and how to use it.

I believe it takes time to know what a good ingredient will actually do. That's why NEUVELIF starts by publishing test results together with their conditions, rather than just ingredient names, and by explaining when and how to use our products after each procedure.
What I realized through this process was simple. In the end, it all came down to wanting to take care of myself. So I defined NEUVELIF's philosophy like this.
Self-care begins with your skin
CEO, NEUVELIF

Epidermal growth factor
A peptide ingredient modeled on a growth factor associated with cells of the epidermis, the skin's outer layer.
What research shows
One study reported improvements in the appearance of fine lines, skin texture, pores, and pigmented spots in 29 women (aged 39–75) who applied a serum containing EGF twice daily for 3 months.
Schouest JM et al., Journal of Drugs in Dermatology, 2012
Insulin-like growth factor
A peptide ingredient modeled on a growth factor structurally similar to insulin.
In skin-aging research, it is described as a growth factor involved in cell growth and division. There are still few studies of it applied to human skin as a cosmetic.
Fibroblast growth factor
A peptide ingredient modeled on a growth factor associated with fibroblasts, the cells that make collagen in the dermis.
